AnovaLab: AnovaLab help 1/9: What one-way ANOVA asks
H₀: every group has the same population mean μ.
ANOVA splits the total spread (SS) in two:
between: n × (group mean - grand mean)²
within: (value - its own group mean)²
MS = SS / df;  F = MS between / MS within.
If H₀ is true, F is near 1 and follows the
F(k - 1, N - k) curve; p = P(F this big | H₀).
A small p is evidence that SOME mean differs:
not which (Pairs page), not how much (eta²).
eta² = SS between / SS total; omega² (Hays)
subtracts the part chance alone would give.
Every value counts: 0 and negatives are data.

AnovaLab help 2/9: Welch and the checks
The F test assumes equal spreads (and roughly normal groups).
Welch's F (1951) drops equal spreads: each group is weighted
by n / s².
Levene's test (Brown-Forsythe form) runs the one-way F on
|value - group median|; non-normal data affect it little.
Bartlett's χ² compares the s² directly: it is misled by
non-normal data.
In the insect-spray preset, s runs from 1.7 to 6.2 and Levene's
test flags it; compare the ordinary F with Welch's.
A check that is not significant is not proof of equal spreads: with
small groups the checks often miss real differences.
Dots page: look at the spreads yourself.

AnovaLab help 3/9: Which pairs differ?
Many t-tests raise the chance of at least one false alarm; these
keep that chance at α for the whole set (the family):
Tukey-Kramer: q = |diff|/√(MSW/2 (1/n₁+1/n₂)) on the
studentized range (it asks before it runs, since it is slow).
Bonferroni: raw t p × m pairs (simple, safe).
Holm: Bonferroni done in steps; never less power than
Bonferroni.

AnovaLab help 6/9: Randomized blocks
Each block (a judge, a person) gets every
treatment once: repeated measures.
Blocks differ a lot, and that spread is taken
OUT of the error: SSE = SST - SSTr - SSBlocks.
F (treatments) = MS treatments / MS error.
partial eta² = SSTr / (SSTr + SSE).
The Table page also shows the one-way F that
ignores the blocks: judges' ratings give
p = 0.048 that way, far smaller with blocks.
Assumes no block × treatment interaction
(and, for repeated measures, sphericity).
Plot: one gray line per block.

AnovaLab help 7/9: One and two variances
One σ: χ² = (n - 1) s² / σ₀², df n - 1.
CI for σ²: ((n-1)s²/χ² upper, (n-1)s²/χ² lower)
Two σ: F = s₁² / s₂², df n₁ - 1 and n₂ - 1.
CI for σ₁²/σ₂²: (F/F upper, F/F lower).
Two-sided p = 2 × the smaller tail.  The curve
shades that tail and the other tail of EQUAL
area (blue), and both critical regions (red).
These tests trust normal data much more than
tests of means do; skewed data mislead them.
For several groups, Levene (Checks) is safer.

ExhibitLab: ExhibitLab help 1/8: What the claim means
'At least 90% are drug, at 95% confidence':
if fewer than 90% of the N units held drug, a random sample of
this size would show this few negatives (or fewer) at most 5% of
the time: the METHOD rarely supports a false claim.  It does NOT
mean: a 95% probability that 90% are drug (a Bayesian
statement, page 2); that the untested units were analyzed; that a
given unit is drug;
anything about weight or purity.
'90%' of 100 units means at least 90 units.
Any key = page 2, Esc = menu
ExhibitLab help 2/8: Frequentist or Bayesian?
Hypergeometric (frequentist): a statement about the PROCEDURE.
Suppose the claim is false by the smallest margin (K₀ drug
units); if what you found would then be rare (P ≤ 1 - c), it is
supported.  Bayesian (Aitken 1999; ENFSI 2009): about THIS
SEIZURE: P(at least p₀N are drug | what you found).  It needs a
prior : uniform Beta(1, 1) treats every proportion as equally
likely; Jeffreys Beta(0.5, 0.5) gives more weight to proportions
near 0 and 1.  The prior matters most when n is small.  Say
which one you used.
Any key = page 3, Esc = menu
ExhibitLab help 3/8: Why N hardly matters
Taking n units out of N barely changes what is left when N is
much bigger than n: the hypergeometric becomes the binomial,
which does not depend on N.  p₀ = 0.90, c = 0.95, no negatives:
the smallest n is 8 at N = 10, 23 at N = 100, never
more than 29 however big N is (computed now; see Tables).
A small seizure needs a large FRACTION tested; a large one about
the same NUMBER.
On the OC page, as N grows, the magenta steps (the
hypergeometric) come to lie on the blue binomial curve.

ExhibitLab help 4/8: Random selection
Every method here assumes the n units were
chosen AT RANDOM: each unit equally likely to
be picked (number them, use random numbers),
not the handiest ones or the top of the bag.
It also assumes the units are alike (if they
differ in look or packing, split them into
groups and sample each: ENFSI), that each
test is right (no false positive or false
negative), and that N was counted correctly.
The claim is about the NUMBER of drug units;
the total weight needs its own estimate.

ExhibitLab help 5/8: The total weight
From the net weights of the n units weighed:
mean , SD s.  Total T = N.  SE =
N s/√n × √((N - n)/N): the finite-population
correction (0 when every unit was weighed;
Cochran; ENFSI s7).  CI: T ± t SE, t on n - 1
df.  A court asks for a LOWER bound: the
total is at least T - t SE (one-sided, at c).
T is the weight of ALL N units; ENFSI s7 also
scales it when some units tested negative
(not done here).  Weights: list D1, a typed
summary, or the example (illustrative).

FitCheck help 2/8: Goodness of fit
χ² GOODNESS OF FIT.  E = N × (the cell's
proportion under H₀): what the cell would hold
if H₀ were exactly right.  χ² = sum of (O -
E)²/E: big when the counts are far from E.  df
= k - 1 - m, where m counts the parameters
estimated from the same data (Poisson λ: 1;
binomial p: 1; normal μ and σ: 2).  p = the
right tail of the χ² curve (Curve page).
Each cell's contribution (O - E)²/E is the
magenta strip under the bars; (O - E)/√E is
its signed square root: beyond ±2 the cell
stands out.

FitCheck help 3/8: Small counts and Merge
The χ² curve gives a trustworthy p only when
the E are not too small: every E ≥ 5, or
Cochran's rule (at most 20% of the E below 5
and none below 1).  FitCheck checks EVERY
cell.  If the rule fails, Merge joins
neighboring cells, the smallest E first, and
the Test page names exactly which cells were
merged (Unmrg undoes it).

FitCheck help 4/8: Benford, Poisson, binomial
BENFORD'S LAW.  In many collections of amounts
spread over several powers of ten the leading
digit d turns up with probability log₁₀(1 +
1/d): a 1 about 30.1% of the time, a 9 only
4.6%.  The first two digits: log₁₀(1 + 1/(10a
+ b)).  In the two-digit test, numbers below
10 are left out (they have no second digit).
Nigrini's MAD is the average gap between the
actual and Benford's proportions.  The orange
curve on the bars is Benford's law.
POISSON: λ is estimated as the mean count; the
last cell is the tail (K or more), so the E
add up to N; df = k - 2.  BINOMIAL: p
estimated (df = k - 2) or typed (df = k - 1).

FitCheck help 5/8: Normality
NORMALITY.  Q-Q plot: each value against its
normal score z (Blom: the N(0,1) quantile at
(i - 3/8)/(n + 1/4)); a normal sample lies
close to the line  + s z.  Shapiro-Wilk W
(Royston 1995): close to 1 for normal data.
Anderson-Darling A² with the correction for
estimated μ and σ (D'Agostino & Stephens
1986): gives extra weight to the tails.
Lilliefors D: the largest gap between the ECDF
and the fitted normal CDF (ECDF page), p by
Dallal & Wilkinson (1986), given for n ≥ 5 and
only below 0.10.  χ² on bins: df = k - 3.

FitCheck help 6/8: Reading p; the exact test
A small p is evidence against normality; a
large p is NOT proof of it.  With a big n,
tiny departures give tiny p: the Q-Q plot
shows how big the departure is.
EXACT BINOMIAL TEST.  X ~ Binomial(n, p₀).
The two-sided p adds P(X = k) over every k no
more likely than the observed x (R's
binom.test, SciPy's binomtest).  Everything is
done in logs, so a p of 10^-145 (the Castaneda
jury preset) is still printed as a number.
The plot shows how many SDs x is from E, the
reasoning the Supreme Court used in Castaneda
v. Partida (1977).

RankLab: RankLab help 1/7: What it does
Rank tests replace each value by its rank, so an outlier counts no
more than the next value, and no normal population is assumed.
Tied values share the average of the ranks they span: the
MIDRANK.  Every test here uses midranks and the
tie-corrected variance.
Each test opens on its Result page.  ⇅ turn the pages: Result, a
picture, the null distribution (and Dunn pairs for Kruskal-
Wallis).  Soft keys: Result, Plot, Null, the 4th key (Exact/Normal,
or what that page switches), Tails, More (Help, Dunn or
Data, Menu).

RankLab help 3/7: Sign test, signed-rank
Both test H₀: the median of d is 0.  Zeros
are dropped: n counts the nonzero d only.
SIGN: S+ = number of d > 0, Binomial(n, 1/2)
under H₀; exact p from BINOMIAL_CDF; two-
sided = 2 × the smaller tail (at most 1).
SIGNED-RANK: rank |d| (midranks); T+ = the
sum of the ranks of d > 0.  Under H₀ each
sign is + or - with chance 1/2, 2^n patterns;
RankLab counts them all (ties too), n ≤ 50.
Effect r = (T+ - T-)/(n(n+1)/2).  Estimate:
Hodges-Lehmann = the median of all Walsh
averages (d_i + d_j)/2, i ≤ j (n ≤ 100).
Page 3/7: key = next, ← = back, Esc = leave
RankLab help 4/7: Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis
MANN-WHITNEY: rank both groups together;
U₁ = R₁ - n₁(n₁ + 1)/2 = the (X, Y) pairs with
X > Y (ties count 1/2).  Exact: every split
of the N ranks is equally likely; RankLab
counts them (no ties, n₁ n₂ ≤ 400).  Ties:
normal, tie-corrected, continuity corrected.
P(X > Y) + ties/2 = U₁/(n₁ n₂); rank-biserial
r = (U₁ - U₂)/(n₁ n₂).  Hodges-Lehmann shift.
KRUSKAL-WALLIS: H compares the k mean ranks;
p from χ²(k - 1); epsilon² = H/(N - 1).
DUNN: z for each pair of mean ranks, Holm-
adjusted over the k(k - 1)/2 pairs.

ResampLab: ResampLab help 1/5: Shuffling labels
A permutation test asks: if the group labels
did not matter (H₀), how often would chance
alone give a difference as big as the one we
saw?
Once: the pooled values are shuffled into new
groups of the same sizes, and the new
difference d is added to the histogram.  Red
line: the observed d; red dots: shuffles at
least as extreme.
p = (as extreme)/(shuffles).  Small p: the
labels seem to matter.  Large p: no evidence
that they do (not proof that they don't).
Assumes: under H₀ the labels could be swapped
without changing anything, which is true when
the groups were made by random assignment.
Any key = page 2
ResampLab help 2/5: Exact, random, paired
EXACT: with few values every split is listed:
C(10, 5) = 252 for two groups of 5, all
counted, so p is exact.  More, then Exact,
shows it.  The limit is 2,000 splits.
RANDOM: otherwise a random sample of B
shuffles estimates p, give or take √(p(1 -
p)/B), and (count + 1)/(B + 1), the plus-one
p, is shown too: never 0, and a valid test.
PAIRED: each pair's difference keeps or flips
its sign at random (blue kept, amber
flipped).  Darwin's 15 pairs: all 2^15 =
32,768 sign patterns are counted exactly, by
their sums.

ResampLab help 3/5: The bootstrap
Treat the sample as the population: draw n
values WITH replacement (a stack of dots = a
value picked more than once) and compute the
statistic.  Repeat B times: their spread
estimates its SE.
Percentile: the middle 95% of the B values.
Basic: the same two ends, mirrored around the
estimate.  BCa: corrected for bias (z₀) and
skew (a); use B ≥ 1,000.  t:  ± t s/√n, to
compare.
Two groups: each resampled from itself;
percentile, and Welch's t for means.
With small samples the intervals are too
narrow: use n of about 15 or more.

ScatterLab: ScatterLab help 1/7: What r measures
r, the correlation, says how closely the
points follow a straight line, and which way.
r near +1: the points rise along a line
r near -1: they fall along a line
r near 0: no STRAIGHT-line pattern -- a
curve can still be there, so look first.
r has no units: crimes per 1,000 or per
100,000 give the same r.  One far-out point
can change r a lot (Menu > far-out point).
r = Sxy / √(Sxx Syy), where
Sxx = sum (x - )², Syy = sum (y - ȳ)²,
Sxy = sum (x - )(y - ȳ).

ScatterLab help 2/7: r², the share explained
All variation in y: SST = sum (y - ȳ)², the squared distances of
the points from the flat line at ȳ.
What the line leaves: SSE = sum (y - ŷ)².
r² = 1 - SSE / SST: the share of the variation in y that the line
accounts for.  r² = 0.64 means 64% explained and 36% left over
in the residuals.  (It is also r times r.)
Try it: Guess starts flat, at ȳ, so 'your SSE' starts at SST.  The best
line brings it down to SSE; the drop, as a share of SST, is r².

ScatterLab help 3/7: Residuals, least squares
residual = observed y - predicted ŷ: the
orange segment from a point to the line
(Resid).  Above the line it is positive.
Least squares picks b₀ and b₁ to make SSE, the
sum of squared residuals, as SMALL as it can:
b₁ = Sxy / Sxx,   b₀ = ȳ - b₁ 
ŷ = b₀ + b₁ x
So the line always passes through the mean
point (, ȳ), the green cross.
Guess: drag the red handles to fit your own
line, then Enter reveals least squares.  No

ScatterLab help 4/7: Leverage
A point far from  has high LEVERAGE: like
a long lever it can swing the whole line.
h = 1/n + (x - )² / Sxx, from 1/n up to 1;
above 4/n (twice the average) counts as high.
Menu > far-out point puts one on the line,
well to the right.  Drag it up and down: the
slope swings.  Drag a point near : the line
lifts a little but barely tilts.
One unusual county can make (or hide) the
whole relationship.  Plot the data and look
before you report r.

ScatterLab help 5/7: Correlation, not causation
r measures association, not cause.  In
summer, ice-cream sales and assaults both
rise -- not because ice cream causes assault,
but because both follow the temperature: a
lurking variable.
Poverty and property crime by county: the
counties also differ in density, policing,
reporting and age mix, and any of these can
drive both.  County figures describe counties,
not people (the ecological fallacy).
The example data are SYNTHETIC: made-up
numbers for practice, not real counties.

ScatterLab help 7/7: Testing the slope
The points are a sample.  Would another sample
give a slope this far from 0?  Menu > Inference
for the slope answers with a t-test:
s = √(SSE / (n - 2)), the typical miss
SE(b₁) = s / √(Sxx),   t = b₁ / SE(b₁)
df = n - 2;  H₀: β₁ = 0;  p is two-tailed
The 95% interval is b₁ ± t crit × SE(b₁).

outer, dotted: where ONE new case would fall

SurvLab: SurvLab help 1/5: Kaplan-Meier curves
Each man is followed until re-arrest (the event,
1) or until follow-up ends (censored, 0).  Rossi's
men were followed 52 weeks; 318 were not re-
arrested: we only know their time is over 52.
At each event time t, with d events among the n
at risk (not yet re-arrested, still followed):
S(t) = S(before t) × (1 - d/n)
the product-limit estimate (Kaplan & Meier 1958).
A censored man counts in n up to his last week,
then leaves: he is never counted as an event.
Greenwood (1926): Var S = S² × sum of d/(n(n - d)).
Ticks on the curve mark censoring times.
Page 1/5, any key = next, Esc = leave
SurvLab help 2/5: CIs, median, quantiles
95% CI, log-log (default): S^exp(±1.96 √V/|ln S|), V = sum of
d/(n(n - d)); it stays inside 0..1.
Linear (soft key CI): S ± 1.96 SE, cut at 0 and 1.
Median: the first time S(t) < 0.5 (statsmodels;
SAS and R average if S sits exactly on 0.5).
If S never gets below 0.5 it is NOT REACHED: in Rossi only 26%
are re-arrested in 52 weeks.  Then report the time by which
25%, 20% or 10% are re-arrested (25%: S = 0.75, the 25th
percentile, or first quartile, of the time to re-arrest).
CI of a quantile (Brookmeyer & Crowley 1982): the event times
whose band reaches S = 1 - p, up to the next event time (not
included); n.r. (not reached) = no upper end.
Cumulative hazard H(t) = sum of d/n (Nelson-Aalen).
Page 2/5, any key = next, Esc = leave
SurvLab help 3/5: Comparing two groups
Log-rank: at each event time, if both groups
shared one curve, group 1 would expect
E₁ = d × n₁/n of the d events.  O = observed.
χ² = (O₁ - E₁)²/V, df 1 (Mantel 1966).
HR = (O₁/E₁)/(O₂/E₂): below 1 = a lower hazard
in group 1; CI exp(ln HR ± 1.96√(1/E₁ + 1/E₂)).
Peto's HR exp((O₁ - E₁)/V) agrees with the test.
Gehan-Breslow weighs each time by n at risk:
early differences count more.  Log-rank is best
for proportional hazards.  Page 3's early/late
line is SurvLab's rule of thumb, not a test.
Assumes: censoring unrelated to the risk; for
the HR, curves that do not cross.

SurvLab help 4/5: The actuarial life table
Intervals [t, t + w) of the width you choose.
n = still at risk at the interval's start,
wdrn = withdrawn (censored) inside it,
n' = n - wdrn/2: a withdrawal is taken to be
at risk for half the interval,
d = events, q = d/n' (conditional probability),
S end = product of (1 - q) so far
(Cutler & Ederer 1958).  Nobody is followed past
the last time, so the last interval ends there,
and those still followed then complete it (not
halved).  Rossi: all 318 not re-arrested were
followed to week 52, so S at 52 = KM's 0.736.
